inserts.title: Leopard alarms draw monkeys into trees
paragraphs: Leopards hunt by ambush on the ground, so a monkey that is feeding or moving low is exposed to attack. In Amboseli, vervet monkeys answered leopard alarms by running into trees. The destination of the escape distinguishes the leopard response from a general reaction to alarm sounds.

Playback used a concealed speaker, and no leopard was present during the trials. Investigators filmed the same recipients before and after each call. Monkeys on the ground ran into trees more often after leopard alarms than after the other alarm categories.

An alarm can therefore start an appropriate escape before any visual identification of the predator. The call guides where the monkey goes as well as how soon it moves. Escape location mattered in these observations, so the sound carried information about refuge as well as danger.

inserts.title: Spectrograms separate the three alarm calls
paragraphs: Leopard, eagle and snake calls from identified monkeys can be displayed on identical time and frequency axes. That shared layout turns each call into a pattern that can be read and compared. Tonal structure, duration and repeated units then stand out in every category.

Eagle alarms showed low-frequency components in these displays. Snake alarms carried a higher-pitched chutter structure, while leopard calls combined short tonal units with repeated sequences. The frequency range shown for the examples ran from 80 to 8000 Hz.

Because the differences are audible, the calls carry acoustic information before any playback begins. Acoustic distinctness gives discrimination a physical basis. Playback experiments then ask how monkeys act once they hear those sounds.

inserts.title: Duration alone leaves category differences intact
paragraphs: Duration is one property that differs between versions of one call. Natural recordings let investigators build short and long versions while preserving the characteristic structure of each alarm category. A longer call often contains more repeated units than a shorter one.

The short stimuli were about 0.3 s long, with one acoustic unit each. The long stimuli ran about 3.7 s and held roughly five units. Each caller contributed matched recordings, which kept caller identity constant across versions, and playback then measured the response to each length.

The category differences survived the change in length. Length therefore contributes less to the response category than other properties do. Urgency and response size, however, can change with length, separately from which action is chosen.

inserts.title: Infants give eagle alarms to many birds
paragraphs: Infant monkeys in Amboseli gave eagle alarms to many birds, and sometimes to harmless objects. Adults limited these alarms to dangerous aerial species, including martial eagles. That narrowing with age is the developmental change documented in this study.

Records from the 14-month study tie each infant, juvenile or adult call to the object that triggered it. Infant errors had structure: aerial objects drew eagle calls, terrestrial mammals drew leopard calls, and long thin objects drew snake calls.

Calls become tied to fewer, more dangerous species as monkeys mature. The change refines categories that infants already use, so the broad categories come first and the narrow ones follow with experience. Juveniles fall between the infant and adult patterns along the same path.

inserts.title: Element duration differs across predator contexts
paragraphs: Duration and spacing make up the temporal side of a call, and energy spread across frequencies makes up the spectral side. The analysis measured both sides in the same recordings, so no single frequency or duration defined an alarm type.

Individual elements were longest in calls given to terrestrial predators. Their mean duration was 107.7 ms. Aerial encounters averaged 43.9 ms and snake encounters averaged 38.3 ms, values that describe single elements rather than whole bouts.

Each feature contributes part of the information in the call, and no single feature forms a perfect boundary. Attributing the discrimination to one feature requires playback in which that feature alone is changed. Such playback tests connect a specific acoustic change to the behavior that follows it.

inserts.title: Aggressive calls overlap predator call forms
paragraphs: Price and colleagues looked at aggressive recordings from both within-group and between-group conflicts. When those calls joined the female predator-call set, snake and aerial calls overlapped with them. A single call type therefore no longer matched a single predator.

The chutter-like snake sounds looked acoustically similar to some intergroup calls. The rraup-like aerial sounds also matched sounds from escalated aggression. Between-group and within-group peak frequencies averaged 1715 Hz and 1456 Hz, values inside the predator range.

Recipients therefore need more than the call form to decide what it means. Additional acoustic details and the immediate social situation give them that information. Each source adds a different kind of information to the same call form. The overlap gives listeners ambiguous cues in some cases.

inserts.title: Male snake and eagle calls share frequencies
paragraphs: In the male recordings, some low-frequency calls appeared in both eagle and snake encounters. The three published clusters lined up only roughly with the predator categories. Some calls appeared in two categories at once. Some calls were therefore shared across predator contexts.

Male element durations averaged 76.5 ms in aerial calls, 61.1 ms in snake calls and 112.0 ms in terrestrial calls. The corresponding peak frequencies were 1090 Hz, 1639 Hz and 1904 Hz, so the two measures separate the contexts together.

Individual calls can land inside the shared range even when the averages differ. Listeners may weigh several features together, along with other environmental cues, when they respond. Averages alone leave some calls in the overlap. Averages describe the recordings, not each individual call.

inserts.title: Male barks occur in leopard and social contexts
paragraphs: Male barks appear in two very different settings, leopard threats and social conflict. Price and colleagues compared real leopard encounters, leopard-model presentations and aggression among males. Each context produced its own acoustic distribution in the analysis.

Acoustic scores for each context form their own distribution, displayed here on a 0.2 s reference scale. The calls from real leopard encounters sit closer to the aggressive barks than the calls from models do. Those distributions overlap in the middle, where the same call form appears in both settings.

The same call form therefore carries information about a social state, not only about a predator. Recipients can use it to learn about either situation. Its meaning therefore depends on the situation in which it is heard. Predator-linked uses are one part of that broader pattern.

inserts.title: Sparse sampling reduces scanner noise
paragraphs: Functional MRI records blood-oxygenation changes that follow neural activity. The scanner is loud, so the stimulus has to be separated from that noise. Sparse sampling places acquisition after a quiet interval, which keeps the stimulus clear of the scanner sound. The stimulus and the scanner noise therefore occupy separate intervals.

Each stimulus was followed by a 6 s delay before the first volume, and every volume lasted 2.18 s. Sound and silence trials alternated, so each response had a silent baseline in the same session. Acquisition followed the stimulus by a fixed interval.

Sparse sampling makes the auditory response measurable in the first place. Localization is the strength of this method, while the timing of a single decision and synaptic detail require other measurements. The strength of the method lies in tracing where sound-driven activity appears.

inserts.title: The right hemisphere shows the larger response
paragraphs: The two sides of the brain can be compared by anatomical section and by regional blood-oxygenation response. Ortiz-Rios and colleagues did this in both macaque hemispheres, so the result rested on measured responses rather than on one visible patch.

In both animals, complex sounds drove a stronger response on the right side under these conditions. Calibration at about 80 dB sound pressure level set the stimulus strength, and silence provided the baseline for each measured value. Both animals showed the same right-side pattern under this design.

The right-side advantage depends on the sounds and the imaging conditions used. Attention differed between the two animals, so each contrast brings out a different part of auditory processing. Response size and behavioral necessity are separate questions that need separate measures.

inserts.title: Anterior temporal regions respond to intact calls
paragraphs: Converging results carry more weight than a single comparison. Ortiz-Rios and colleagues combined two contrasts, call versus environmental sound and call versus scrambled call, then searched for regions that responded to both in the macaques.

The shared region sat in the anterior temporal cortex, including lateral rostrotemporal areas and the rostrotemporal pole. Stimuli were 8 s sequences, and acquisition began 6 s in, which set the timing of each measured response. The map then places that response on the anatomy.

Convergence across two independent controls narrows the explanation toward vocal processing. Environmental sounds alone would give a broader picture, which is why the two-control design matters. Each control removes a different alternative explanation.

inserts.title: Leopard chirps are longer, with higher peaks
paragraphs: Leopard and snake models each elicited chirps in this green-monkey study, and the chirps were analyzed by context. Duration and an early peak-frequency measure together did most of the work of separating the two groups. The chirps were analyzed as continuous measurements rather than as fixed types.

Chirps given to leopard models lasted longer and reached a higher early peak than those given to snake models. Scores were tabulated in milliseconds and Hz, and their distributions formed a continuum between the two groups. Many individual chirps sat in the middle of that range.

The physical variation is present in the sounds themselves. Whether a listener treats a middle chirp as a leopard threat, a snake threat or a reason to inspect depends on reception and decision processes beyond the acoustic analysis. Physical differences set the input, and the listener's processes set the decision.

inserts.title: Prior predator evidence extends time in trees
paragraphs: Persistence and immediate climbing answer different questions about the same broad alarm. One asks what a monkey does first, and the other asks how long it stays in the tree. Prior evidence can affect the second even when the first follows the acoustics.

When both the leopard model and the leopard chirps signaled terrestrial danger, subjects remained in trees longer. Persistence meant staying more than 200 s, whereas the immediate response meant climbing above 2 m after the broadcast.

Early action follows the call's acoustics, while persistence also reflects earlier information about the threat. The two measures therefore differ in what they reveal about the same call. Each measure adds its own information to that call. Both measures were taken from the same subjects in the same study.
notes: Prior predator evidence extends time in trees.

inserts.title: Ongoing conflict reduces looking at the caller
paragraphs: Looking toward a caller can help a listener work out what caused an alarm. Deshpande and colleagues played the same male bark to recipients, with and without an intergroup encounter going on, and timed how long each one looked at the speaker.

Looks were longest when the surrounding situation contained no conflict. Times were recorded in seconds across 10 min of field observation. Social activity already explained the barking during an encounter, which may reduce the need to look toward the speaker.

Integrating the bark with the surrounding social context shapes how long recipients keep looking. Reading the longer looks as uncertainty is a proposed interpretation, and it sits apart from any measured mental state. The social setting alone changes between the two conditions.

2: **Alarm calls** are vocal signals tied to particular dangers. Free-ranging vervet monkeys, now named _Chlorocebus pygerythrus_, gave distinct calls when they met terrestrial predators, aerial predators or snakes. Field recordings and observations made over 14 months in Amboseli, Kenya, identified these three categories.

Seyfarth, Cheney and Marler broadcast recorded calls when no predator was present. Monkeys changed where they looked and how they escaped according to the call type, within a 10 s window. Hearing an alarm therefore produced a response even without seeing the predator that usually causes it.

**Referential signaling** carries information about things and happenings in the external world. Responses that match each predator support a functional reading of the calls. Whether a caller intends to describe a predator, or a listener forms a symbolic representation of one, is a distinct question.
3: **Leopards** are terrestrial ambush predators, so an attack can reach a monkey that is moving or feeding on the ground. In Amboseli, alarm calls linked to leopards were followed by movement into trees. The escape destination, more than movement itself, defined the response.

Investigators played the calls through a hidden speaker when no leopard was present, then filmed each recipient before and after the sound. Monkeys on the ground were more likely to run into trees after leopard alarms than after the other alarm categories. Each animal was measured against its own earlier behavior.

An alarm alone can start an appropriate escape before a predator is visually identified. The sound therefore supplies information about where to go as well as when to move, which provides an acoustic route into defensive action. The first movement can therefore be triggered by hearing alone.
4: Martial eagles attack from above, so looking upward and reaching protective cover answer a different threat from climbing away from a leopard. Observers in the same habitat recorded the eagle-associated calls while tracking each monkey's position and subsequent actions.

Playback without an eagle present caused ground-dwelling monkeys to look upward, and some ran into cover. Monkeys already up in trees could come down and leave. Responses in the 10 s after each playback were judged against the 10 s that preceded it.

Where a monkey sits determines how exposed it is, so the same call can lead to different actions. A shared call category therefore allows several motor sequences, and the responses still reveal that monkeys distinguish aerial danger from ground threats.
5: Snake alarms were high-pitched, chutter-like calls given in response to pythons and other threatening snakes. A threat on the ground calls for a different reaction than an attack from the air, so looking down and approaching the snake differed from escaping up a tree.

Predator-free playbacks of snake calls produced more ground-directed looking than the other call types did. Scoring compared each monkey's behavior before and after the broadcast, using one 10 s window. A speaker supplied the sound, and no physical snake was present.

**Ground-directed inspection** gathers information about a threat that is close by. Calling, looking, approaching and escaping are separate components of the response, and each can occur on its own. Inspection can therefore come before any escape.
6: A **spectrogram** plots acoustic energy against time and frequency. The classic recordings compared leopard, eagle and snake calls from identified adults and one juvenile. Tonal structure, duration and repeated acoustic units become visible on the two axes, which makes the categories straightforward to compare.

The examples were analyzed with a 300 Hz filter and displayed between 80 and 8000 Hz. Eagle alarms carry **low-frequency components**. Snake alarms have a higher-pitched chutter pattern, and leopard calls combine short tonal units with repeated sequences. Each category has a recognizable acoustic signature.

Field listeners detected these differences as well, so the distinctions exist in the sounds the monkeys hear. Acoustic distinctness provides a basis for discrimination. Playback experiments then test how the monkeys respond, which supplies the behavioral side of the same question.
7: An **acoustic unit** is a single sound element, whereas a **sequence** contains several elements. Adult male leopard alarms often consist of repeated units. Female and juvenile leopard alarms can instead consist of one short element, even though the same predator category elicits them.

Seyfarth and colleagues sampled identified individuals instead of assuming that one waveform represents the entire population. Their spectrograms use 0.5 s time scales. Some females also gave multi-unit leopard calls, particularly when a predator was close or attacking. This sampling made variation among callers visible.

Call category and detailed acoustic form describe the same signal at two levels. Callers can therefore differ in form while sharing one behavioral function, and both descriptions remain useful. A category label summarizes the function, while the acoustic form records how the sound is built.
8: **Playback** presents a recorded signal to measure its effect on a listener. In the classic field experiment, a speaker was hidden, and leopard, eagle or snake alarms were broadcast when no predator was visible. The orientation of the speaker and the order of calls changed from trial to trial.

The Science report measured the 10 s before each broadcast and the 10 s after it. Ground responses included escape into trees, seeking cover, and looking up or down. Table 1 also sorts monkeys already in trees from monkeys on the ground.

Removing the predator rules out the idea that recipients copied responses to something they could see. The call still carries its acoustic and social information. A response to sound therefore shows what the listener receives, while the caller's own motives need separate observations.
9: **Call duration** is the time a vocalization occupies, and longer calls often include more repeated units. Natural recordings allowed the investigators to build short and long versions of each call. Both versions kept the structure typical of their alarm category.

Short stimuli lasted 0.3 s on average and contained a single acoustic unit. Long stimuli averaged 3.7 s and contained roughly five units. Matched recordings from one caller helped separate duration from caller identity, and playback measured the defensive response to each version.

Changing duration left the main differences among leopard, eagle and snake responses intact. Duration by itself therefore explains little of these category differences. Urgency and response magnitude still change with duration, independent of which action is chosen.
10: **Amplitude** describes how loud a sound is, whereas acoustic structure covers the frequency distribution and timing pattern of a call. The natural calls varied in loudness. Reconstructed field playback levels averaged 56 dB for leopard alarms, 53 dB for eagle alarms and 48 dB for snake alarms.

The investigators also sorted responses where amplitude ranges overlapped, and they ran trials with equalized amplitude. Category differences in defensive behavior held up in both analyses. These controls indicate that the categories reflect different kinds of action rather than a general disturbance from louder sounds.

Sound level therefore falls short as a full explanation for the category-specific actions in this preparation. Sound level, caller state and external danger can change together, yet each one contributes its own variable to the response. Each variable is measured separately, so the response can be attributed to its own source.
11: **Context** includes the recipient's surroundings and position when a signal arrives. The classic experiments tested ground-dwelling subjects and tree-dwelling subjects, so the same alarm category was evaluated where refuge and vulnerability differed. Position therefore becomes part of the stimulus.

Ground subjects commonly moved upward after leopard alarms. Eagle alarms could make tree-dwelling monkeys leave the tree. Each 10 s scoring window set these actions against the individual's own behavior before playback, so every movement was classified separately.

A stable link between an alarm and a danger class is compatible with context-dependent action. The same external threat can call for different movements from different starting points. Different calls also produced contrasting responses in one setting, so context shaped the action without replacing the call's information.
12: **Ontogeny** refers to change during an individual's development. In Amboseli, infants gave eagle alarms to many birds and sometimes to harmless objects. Adult callers restricted these alarms more strongly to dangerous aerial species, including martial eagles. The narrowing took place over the course of development.

Alarms collected over 14 months show the stimuli linked to infant, juvenile and adult calling. Infant errors were systematic. Aerial stimuli usually drew eagle calls, terrestrial mammals usually drew leopard calls, and long thin objects usually drew snake calls.

The developmental pattern fits refinement within broad perceptual categories. Infants already sort threats into those categories, and experience narrows which stimuli trigger each call. Juvenile patterns fall between the infant and adult patterns.
13: **Predator classification** assigns encountered objects to threat categories. Adults met many harmless species without alarming, and they called more selectively to predators relevant to their habitat. Earlier developmental observations set these narrower adult associations against the broad categories of infants.

The eagle-alarm data cover raptors, other birds, and a few additional stimuli. Records gathered during a 14-month field study tied each call to the object that elicited it. Juvenile patterns fell between the broad infant pattern and the selective adult pattern.

The change concerns when existing calls are used, rather than the acquisition of new acoustic forms. Calls are used in narrower settings as monkeys mature, and age-related refinement supports experience-sensitive categorization in these callers.
14: An **acoustic cluster** groups calls with similar measured properties before any predator name is assigned. Price and colleagues analyzed recordings made during predator encounters and aggressive interactions. Female calls fell into four broad groups that differed in element length and frequency distribution.

Spectrograms show frequency in kHz and time in seconds, with representative elements drawn on 0.2 s scales. Some clusters contained repeated short sounds, while one terrestrial-predator cluster contained fewer and longer elements. The analysis built upon earlier qualitative descriptions.

Clustering reveals organization in the recorded repertoire, which describes how calls are produced. Acoustically similar sounds can occur in more than one behavioral setting, so the number of clusters belongs to the recordings themselves. Clusters therefore summarize production before any meaning is assigned.
15: **Temporal features** describe duration and spacing, whereas **spectral features** describe how energy is spread across frequencies. Price and colleagues measured both kinds, instead of defining alarm types from one frequency or one duration. The examples keep their original kHz and second scales.

Calls given to terrestrial predators by females contained longer single elements than calls for aerial and snake encounters. Mean element durations were 107.7 ms for terrestrial encounters, 43.9 ms for aerial encounters and 38.3 ms for snake encounters. These values refer to single elements, not complete alarm bouts.

Several features can support discrimination together, even when no single measure draws a perfect boundary between categories. Controlled changes to playback stimuli are the method for attributing discrimination to one feature. Such experiments turn a correlation in the recordings into a tested link between sound and response.
16: **Production specificity** is the link between a signal and the situations in which it is produced. Limiting the analysis to predator encounters, Price and colleagues compared female calls recorded during aerial, snake and terrestrial threats. The acoustic distributions for these three contexts separated strongly.

Spectral measurements help separate these contexts. Average peak frequencies came to 986 Hz in aerial calls, 2840 Hz in snake calls and 2374 Hz in terrestrial calls. Temporal structure also differed, so peak frequency was one feature among several in the classification.

The distinctions hold among the three predator contexts in this data set. Aggressive encounters were analyzed separately, in a later comparison of the same recordings. Specificity therefore depends on which alternative situations the analysis includes.
17: A **call element** is a component within a compound vocalization, and a bout can contain several successive vocalizations. Price and colleagues separated measures of the whole call from spectral measures of its individual elements. This avoids assuming that every duration refers to the same biological unit.

Snake-linked calls from females had more brief elements than calls linked to terrestrial predators. Mean element numbers were 4.1 for snake calls and 1.4 for terrestrial calls. Mean element durations were 38.3 ms and 107.7 ms, so the two arrangements gave contrasting temporal patterns.

These measurements connect acoustic organization to the eliciting context without equating each call with a fixed word. A listener could combine the pattern with frequency and social cues. The temporal pattern and the frequency content are two inputs the listener can use together.
18: **Aggression** consists of antagonistic interactions within groups or between them. Price and colleagues included these aggressive recordings in the analysis of female predator calls. Calls linked to snakes and aerial predators then overlapped with aggressive calls, which weakens a simple one-call, one-predator description.

Snake calls with a chutter-like sound resembled some intergroup calls. Aerial calls with a rraup-like sound resembled calls given during escalated aggression. Mean peak frequencies during between-group and within-group aggression were 1715 Hz and 1456 Hz, both inside the wider range of predator-associated calls.

Acoustic structure often matches several contexts at once, so context must be inferred from more than one feature. Recipients also weigh further acoustic details and the current situation, and those factors can shape how they respond to the same call.
19: **Graded variation** consists of intermediate forms along acoustic dimensions. Discrete categories, by contrast, have clearer boundaries between them. Female chutter-like and rraup-like calls occupied overlapping acoustic space once aggressive contexts were added, and the distributions come from measured features rather than hand-assigned word equivalents.

The spectrograms preserve 0.2 s time scales and frequency axes in kHz. They reveal repeated-element patterns whose measured distributions overlap. Calls from the same broad acoustic region occurred during snake encounters, aerial encounters and social aggression. Each context contributed calls to that shared region.

Overlapping production distributions are compatible with categorical perception by listeners. Establishing that perception would require a reception experiment that measures responses across controlled acoustic variation. Such an experiment would show where listeners draw category boundaries within the continuum.
20: Researchers analyzed male and female calls on separate tracks because the two sexes produced quite different structures. In East African males, Price and colleagues found three clusters, while females had four. The male groups varied in how their elements repeat and in how energy spreads across frequency.

The male spectrograms use second and kHz scales, with sounds shown against 0.2 s intervals. One group contained many short high-frequency elements. Another held fewer, longer elements, and a third had low-frequency components. Their links to predator contexts varied in how exclusive they were.

Sex-specific organization makes a recording from one caller a poor stand-in for the whole alarm repertoire. Body characteristics, vocal mechanics and contextual usage are possible contributors to the difference. Each of these explanations predicts a different pattern across callers.
21: **Acoustic overlap** happens when distinct eliciting situations yield similar spans of measured call features. In male data, some low-frequency calls occurred during both eagle and snake encounters. The published clusters therefore matched the three predator categories imperfectly, with some calls appearing in two of them.

Male elements averaged 76.5 ms in aerial calls, 61.1 ms in snake calls and 112.0 ms in terrestrial calls. Male peak frequencies averaged 1090 Hz, 1639 Hz and 1904 Hz, in the same order. Duration and frequency together describe these contrasts.

Average values differ across contexts, but individual calls can fall into the overlap. A listener may integrate several features with environmental information. Playback experiments with particular recipients show how that ambiguity shapes defensive behavior in a given setting.
22: **Frequency range** is the span of frequencies present in a measured call element. Price and colleagues set this measure beside temporal organization and energy distribution in male alarms. The recorded calls varied by context along several dimensions at once.

Mean frequency ranges were 1832 Hz for aerial calls, 4069 Hz for snake calls and 3794 Hz for terrestrial calls. The spectrograms keep frequency and time scales, so the spectral differences can be related to the temporal pattern of each call.

Frequency range is a physical property of the sound, measured the same way in every context. Snake and terrestrial calls had similar ranges, and both were broader than aerial calls. The measure captures the sound itself, so any link to threat level must come from behavior.
23: An **acoustic classifier** assigns recordings to groups on the basis of measured features. Price and colleagues evaluated how well predator context could be separated in male calls, and they added checks that reduced the chance that caller identity alone explained the result. This analysis of recordings differs from a playback test.

Terrestrial-associated male calls separated more clearly from the others. Some snake and aerial recordings occupied overlapping parts of acoustic space. Terrestrial calls therefore form the clearest group among these male recordings. The spectrograms use 0.2 s scales and kHz frequency axes.

A classifier's success measures the information present in the recordings under the chosen measurements. Behavioral responses and neural recordings address the later stages that link acoustic information to an inferred external event. Each stage uses a different measurement, so each answers a separate question.
24: **Barks** are a male call form associated with terrestrial threats and also with antagonistic interactions. Price and colleagues analyzed South African recordings made during actual leopard encounters, leopard-model presentations and social aggression. These contexts gave overlapping acoustic distributions.

Calls to real leopards resembled aggressive barks more closely than calls elicited by leopard models did, within the available recordings. Acoustic scores were summarized as a distribution for each context, shown against a 0.2 s reference scale. The leopard-model calls therefore matched the social barks less closely.

A bark can signal a social state as well as a predator, and recipients can use it as information about either. Predator-linked meaning therefore accounts for part of how this call form is used. Predator and social uses share one acoustic form, so the form serves both meanings.
25: **Affective state** describes an animal's emotional or motivational condition, and **cognitive appraisal** describes its evaluation of a situation. Price and colleagues proposed that both could shape call structure and use, since acoustically similar male barks occurred with predators and in social aggression.

The recorded distributions contrast real leopard encounters, leopard models and aggressive encounters, with spectrograms on a 0.2 s timescale. The acoustic overlap is the measured finding. A shared internal state that links those contexts is a plausible explanation, suggested by that overlap.

Information about an external event and information about internal state can both appear in one call. Identifying the neurotransmitter, receptor or ion channel behind either contribution would require direct measurements in the callers.
26: **Conspecific vocalizations** are calls produced by members of the listener's own species. Ortiz-Rios and colleagues tested rhesus macaque calls against environmental sounds and scrambled calls during functional MRI. These experiments in macaques supply comparative neural evidence, drawn from a species other than vervets.

Stimuli were grouped into 8 s sequences and played at roughly 80 dB sound pressure level. Scrambling shuffled 200 ms segments across time and frequency, which kept much of each segment's local structure. Environmental sounds provided a second class of complex natural sounds.

Comparing these conditions tests whether activation reflects hearing complex sound or sensitivity to intact vocal patterns. The responses concern macaque auditory processing, so a link to a vervet alarm-decoding circuit is a separate step, and that circuit would need its own measurements.
27: **Functional MRI** tracks blood-oxygen changes rather than the firing of individual neurons. The scanner itself makes noise. Ortiz-Rios and colleagues used sparse sampling, which places silent intervals between acquisitions and leaves gaps for stimulation, to reduce interference from scanner noise.

Image acquisition began 6 s after each stimulus onset, and each volume took 2.18 s. Sound conditions alternated with silent trials. One macaque performed an auditory task with eye movements, while the other listened during steady fixation, so attention varied between the two animals.

The delayed blood-oxygenation signal localizes sound-sensitive regions. The timing of a single alarm decision is much faster than this signal, so synaptic sign, transmitter release and receptor activation need measurements beyond this imaging approach.
28: The **ascending auditory pathway** carries sound-related signals through brainstem, thalamic and cortical stations. In awake macaques, Ortiz-Rios and colleagues contrasted complex sounds with silence and placed the activation on anatomical MRI sections. The maps covered the inferior colliculus, the medial geniculate and auditory cortex.

The **inferior colliculus** is a midbrain auditory region, and the **medial geniculate nucleus** is the auditory relay in the thalamus. Functional images used voxels of 1.5 × 1.5 × 1.9 mm. At that size, each voxel pools signals from many cells and their blood vessels.

These regions responded to several categories of complex sound, so they supply anatomical context for signal reception rather than a call-specific map. Their activity fits a pathway that carries sound toward the cortex. Each region along that route belongs to the reception stage.
29: **Primary auditory cortex**, also called A1, is the cortical area that receives heavy ascending auditory input. **Belt** and **parabelt** label neighboring auditory cortical areas. Ortiz-Rios and colleagues mapped complex-sound activation onto anatomical surfaces and saw responses across these auditory territories.

The 8 s sound sequences were contrasted with silence, so the broad activation reflects auditory stimulation in general. Responses also reached along the **superior temporal gyrus**, a cortical ridge with auditory and auditory-associated regions.

An anatomical activation map shows the location of a measured response. Each colored region may perform a different computation, and selectivity for intact calls depends on comparisons with matched non-call or scrambled-call controls. The map sets the spatial scope of the response, not its function.
30: **Hemispheric lateralization** is an unequal contribution or measured response from the two sides of the brain. Ortiz-Rios and colleagues compared auditory activation in both macaque hemispheres, using anatomical sections and regional blood-oxygenation responses instead of a single visible patch.

Both animals responded more strongly to complex sounds in the right hemisphere under these conditions. The sounds were calibrated to roughly 80 dB, and silence trials supplied the baseline. The pattern held for the tested sound set and imaging conditions.

The larger right-hemisphere response reflects this sound set and these imaging conditions. Attention differed between the two animals, and each contrast emphasizes a different part of auditory processing. Regional response size and behavioral necessity are separate empirical questions, each measured in its own way.
31: The **superior temporal gyrus** contains auditory-associated cortex, and its anterior portion lies toward the front of the temporal lobe. Ortiz-Rios and colleagues compared intact macaque calls with scrambled versions to find where local acoustic similarity failed to explain the response.

Scrambling assembled 200 ms tiles, each spanning one **octave** of frequency. An octave is a doubling or halving of frequency, and here it sets the spectral width of each tile. Intact calls evoked stronger responses than scrambled controls in anterior temporal regions, including rostrotemporal areas.

The result indicates sensitivity to organized vocal patterns beyond some preserved local sound features. The responses were recorded in macaques, so they point to processing of vocal organization rather than to a neuron that represents a predator.
32: **Ventrolateral prefrontal cortex** is a frontal cortical area, and **ventral premotor cortex** takes part in sensorimotor processing. Imaging contrasts between calls and environmental sounds produced activation in frontal and parietal cortex as well as in temporal auditory regions.

The environmental sounds were complex natural recordings, but their **spectrotemporal** patterns were distinct from the calls. Spectrotemporal structure describes how acoustic energy changes across frequency and time together. The 200 ms scrambling control kept more of the calls' local sound properties than it kept of the environmental sounds.

Scrambled calls also activated some frontal and parietal regions. A response to a call can therefore arise from acoustics, task demands or associated processing. Each contrast mixes several sources of activity in the same regions.
33: A **conjunction analysis** identifies regions that meet more than one comparison, so a result must hold across several controls. Ortiz-Rios and colleagues combined call-versus-environmental-sound and call-versus-scrambled-call comparisons, then looked for convergence across the macaques.

The strongest shared result involved anterior temporal regions, including lateral rostrotemporal cortex and the rostrotemporal pole. Stimuli were presented as 8 s sequences, with acquisition starting after 6 s. The map shows the blood-oxygenation response that survives both comparisons.

This convergence supports a narrower vocal-processing interpretation than the broader environmental-sound contrast alone provides. Comparative auditory specialization narrows the plausible explanations for how macaque brains process communication sounds. Two independent controls agreeing gives the result more weight than either control alone.
34: _Chlorocebus sabaeus_, the West African green monkey, is closely related to vervets, yet it is a separate species in this study. Price and Fischer presented leopard and snake models in Senegal and filmed the first 10 s of each subject's response to the detected model.

Leopard models elicited more tree climbing than snake models did. Standing bipedally appeared in both threat settings, so it was a shared posture rather than a snake-specific one. The researchers recorded movement and maximum height, which distinguished refuge selection from posture and general inspection.

The model experiment established which behaviors are appropriate for interpreting this population's playback responses. Posture meanings are therefore set within this green monkey population, using the behaviors observed during model encounters. Those measured behaviors then serve as the reference for each playback result.
35: **Chirps** are the call form that the green-monkey predator experiments examined. Both females and juveniles gave chirps in response to leopard and snake models. Price and Fischer built paired playback sequences from recordings of the two eliciting conditions, so the calls were treated as graded variants of one family.

Spectrograms show time in seconds and frequency in kHz. Paired sequences were matched for chirp number, inter-call interval and total sequence duration, with intervals constrained to naturally occurring values. Recordings were normalized before they were broadcast.

These controls rule out explanations based solely on bout length or repeated-call number. Frequency distribution and element duration varied together in the natural recordings, so several dimensions covary with the predator distinction. Graded differences within each chirp stayed available to listeners.
36: Graded acoustic categories can overlap considerably even when their average structures differ. Price and Fischer examined chirps from green monkeys that leopard and snake models had elicited. Duration and an early peak-frequency measure contributed most to separating the recordings.

Chirps linked to leopards lasted longer and showed a higher early peak frequency than chirps linked to snakes. Durations were measured in milliseconds and frequencies in Hz. Their score distributions overlapped, forming a continuum rather than two fully separate groups.

The findings show variation that can be detected physically within one broad call form. How a recipient responds to an intermediate chirp, as a leopard threat, a snake threat or a cue to inspect, depends on reception and decision processes. The acoustic analysis captures the input, not the decision.
37: An **experimental control** rules out a competing explanation for an observed response. Price and Fischer broadcast nonpredatory bird calls alongside the green-monkey chirp stimuli. The bird calls served as a control for the playback procedure itself, rather than as another predator-associated monkey signal.

Monkeys responded more often to chirps than to bird sounds. Playback levels stayed in the range of natural calls, 60–85 dB measured at 10 m from the speaker. A different recording sequence was used in each experiment, so no single exemplar was tested repeatedly.

The contrast shows that the monkeys responded to biologically relevant acoustic information, not to any sound from the speaker. Whether the recipient represents a predator, experiences conditioned danger or combines both is a question about interpretation beyond the procedural control.
38: **Priming** provides relevant information ahead of a later test. Price and Fischer exposed green monkeys to a leopard model, a snake model or no predator model, and then broadcast chirps. The calls were played about 1 h after each model presentation, once alarm calling had stopped.

The design varied the preceding model independently of the original context of each recorded chirp. Chirps linked to leopards more often prompted climbing above 2 m than chirps linked to snakes. The prior model left the immediate response category largely unchanged.

Acoustic cues therefore strongly shaped the early action in this preparation. Information presented an hour earlier can influence later persistence in a different way from the first movement after a call. The first movement is driven mainly by the call's acoustic features.
39: **Response persistence** is the time an action or defensive state continues after it begins. Price and Fischer separated immediate tree climbing from staying in a tree after playback. These two measures capture different consequences of hearing the same broad alarm form.

Subjects stayed in trees longer when leopard-model exposure and leopard-associated chirps both signaled terrestrial danger. The persistence measure recorded whether a subject stayed more than 200 s. The immediate measure recorded climbing above 2 m following the broadcast.

Prior information contributes to sustained risk assessment, even when early action follows mainly from the acoustics. The two measures therefore carry different information about the same call. Early action follows the call's acoustics, while persistence also reflects earlier information.
40: South African male vervets produce similar alarm barks when a terrestrial predator appears and during conflict between groups. Deshpande and colleagues tested whether recipients used the current social situation to interpret the sound. The stimuli were one predator-associated bark and one intergroup bark from the same adult male.

Each female recipient heard the same assigned recording in both contexts, played at a natural amplitude from a speaker 30–50 m away. This within-recipient design keeps the stimulus fixed while the surrounding intergroup situation changes. Spectrograms show seconds and frequency in Hz.

Holding the recording constant isolates the effect of context from differences between sounds used on different occasions. The experiment tests this call with these receivers under specified field conditions. Each receiver therefore serves as its own comparison across the two situations.
41: An **intergroup encounter** takes place when members of neighboring monkey groups interact. Deshpande and colleagues tested recipients away from the conflict front while the encounter was ongoing. Subjects stayed at least 30 m from the front and were foraging, resting or grooming.

The same recipients were also tested with no intergroup encounter, at least 2 h after the last such event or natural alarm call. Habitat and approximate group spread were matched, and playback came from 30–50 m away. The same playback distance applied in both conditions.

This manipulation supplies immediate contextual information, whereas the earlier model exposure occurred about 1 h before the green-monkey playbacks. Timing and call type were both changed between the two studies, so different outcomes are expected.
42: **Information seeking** can involve orienting toward a caller to gather more cues about an alarm's cause. Deshpande and colleagues measured how long recipients looked toward the speaker after hearing the same male bark, both with and without an ongoing intergroup encounter.

Recipients generally looked at the speaker for longer when no intergroup encounter was underway. Looking time was measured in seconds across 10 min of field observation after playback. During an encounter, surrounding social activity already offered a plausible reason for the barking.

The measured effect indicates that acoustic and contextual information are combined. Longer looking is a proposed sign of uncertainty, a reading of the behavior rather than a measured mental state. The change appears within the same bark, which suggests the context itself is doing the work.
43: **Vigilance** is monitoring of the surroundings while maintaining an alert posture. Deshpande and colleagues measured vigilance duration apart from speaker-directed looking, startle and predator-specific escape. Female recipients were more vigilant after barks given outside an intergroup encounter than during one.

Vigilance durations were recorded in seconds. Some recipients showed no vigilance during the encounter condition, even though every one of them heard the bark. Predator-specific escape occurred in neither condition, and startle was recorded as a sudden body movement.

Defensive responses can change in intensity without turning into overt flight. Altered monitoring of the surroundings and of the presumed caller shows context-sensitive reception in these females. The alert posture changes while the animals stay in place.
44: **Social learning** is behavioral change supported by information from other individuals. Mohr and colleagues showed unfamiliar raptor models to juvenile vervets, 1–2 years old, while watching nearby audiences. The juveniles could watch both the model and the reactions of other monkeys.

Juveniles sometimes alarmed to these models, whereas adults remained silent. Audience members were individuals within 10 m of the subject. The result matches the classic age pattern, in which more experienced adults judge unfamiliar models differently from younger animals.

Caller age and alarm production were associated in these observations. The developmental difference concerns calling behavior, and it is a separate matter from any age-specific neural circuit. The data set compares callers of different ages in the same setting.
45: An **audience effect** is a change in signaling linked to who is nearby. Mohr and colleagues contrasted juvenile calling when mothers, siblings or unrelated group members were present within 10 m. Other relatives were left out of the mother and sibling conditions, which kept the audience categories apart.

The descriptive pattern showed more juvenile calling with siblings than with mothers or unrelated animals. Mothers and siblings also directed their vigilance toward the model, which supplied extra social information that the juveniles could use during each trial.

These observations motivate explanations that involve experience, relatedness or awareness. A difference in immediate calling is a different measure from a lasting acquired association, so the design supports a developmental interpretation of the calling pattern.
